Recurrent Neural Networks · Part 4

Look back while you write

Attention: the decoder keeps the input open, and picks what to read at every step.

Part 3 ended on a limit: the whole input had to fit through one c. Today the decoder stops relying on that one summary. While it writes each word, it looks back over the whole input sentence and decides which words matter right now. The picture is the whole talk: writing "chat", most of its attention goes to "cat".

Where we left off

One c was too small

Part 3's date translator, reading more dates through the same c:

1 date99%
2 dates1%
4 dates0%
  1. One summary for any length. c is the same size for 3 words or 45.
  2. The decoder can't look back. After the hand-off it never sees the input again.
  3. Early words fade. The first word must survive every encoder step to reach c.

The encoder computed a memory hj after every character. Part 3 threw all but the last one away.

Quick recap, two minutes. The bars are measured: demo/seq2seq.py with --max-dates 4. The three limits are the ones from the end of Part 3. The callout is the key observation that leads straight to attention: the information we need was computed, we just discarded it.

The idea

Keep every memory, and look up the one you need

Part 3 · from memory

Hear the whole speech once, then translate it with no notes. Whatever you didn't remember is gone.

Part 4 · with the text open

Keep the original in front of you. Before each word you write, glance back at the part you're translating now.

  • The encoder doesn't change. We just keep h1 … hT instead of only hT.
  • At every step, the decoder builds a fresh context ct: a mix of the hj, weighted by how useful each one is right now.
  • The weights are called attention. Nobody tells the model where to look. It learns that from the translation loss alone.
This is the slide to say out loud in an interview: "instead of one fixed context vector, the decoder computes a new context at every step as a weighted average of all the encoder's hidden states, and the weights are learned". The three bullets answer the three limits from the last slide in order. Point out that each h_j isn't just "character j": it's the encoder's memory after reading up to j, so it carries some context from before it.

A little history

From one paper to every modern model

2014Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio, Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate. The encoder–decoder from Part 3, plus attention. Its quality holds up on long sentences where the basic model's falls off.
2015Minh-Thang Luong, Hieu Pham and Christopher Manning, Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation: simpler ways to score (a dot product). Kelvin Xu and colleagues, Show, Attend and Tell: attention over the parts of an image, for captions.
2016Yonghui Wu and colleagues (Google), Google's Neural Machine Translation System: Google Translate switches to an LSTM encoder–decoder with attention.
2017Ashish Vaswani and colleagues, Attention Is All You Need: keep the attention, drop the RNN. The Transformer.

Orange: authors · blue: paper titles

Bahdanau et al. called it "align and translate": the weights line up each output word with input words. The paper's title in full is worth knowing for an interview. Luong et al. (2015, "Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation") compared scoring functions; the dot product is the one Transformers use. Xu et al. (2015, "Show, Attend and Tell") showed the idea isn't about text. The 2016 system is Google's Neural Machine Translation (GNMT, Wu et al.). We'll come back to 2017 at the end.

How it works · one decoder step

Score, soften, mix

1
Score each input memory: how useful is it for what I'm about to write?
ej = score(st−1, hj)
2
Soften the scores into weights: positive, adding up to 1.
aj = softmax(e)j
3
Mix: the context for this step is the weighted average.
ct = a1h1 + a2h2 + … + aThT
Three verbs to remember: score, soften, mix. The decoder's memory from the previous step, s_{t−1}, says what it's looking for; each h_j says what's there. Then c_t goes into the decoder alongside the previous output word, exactly where Part 3 used c. This happens at EVERY decoder step, with a different s each time, so a different mix each time. Softmax is the same function that turns the decoder's output scores into chances, from Part 1.

Try it · softmax

Turn scores into weights

The decoder is about to write chat. Drag the scores and watch the weights.

inputscore ejweight aj

Only differences between scores matter. Big gaps give sharp focus on one word; equal scores give a plain average.

Let someone drive. Things to find: (1) adding the same amount to every score changes nothing; (2) all equal gives one third each, which is just an average of the memories, closer to Part 3's single summary; (3) a gap of about 3 already puts most of the weight on one word. Softmax: a_j = exp(e_j) / Σ_k exp(e_k). The weights are never exactly 0, so every input word gets a little say; that matters for training, because blame can then reach every word.

How it scores

A tiny network asks: “is this what I need?”

ej = v · tanh( Ws st−1 + Wh hj )
Ws st−1

What the decoder needs now. “I've written 2026-10-; I need the day.”

Wh hj

What's at input position j. “I'm the memory just after reading 23.”

v · tanh(…)

How well they match, as one number. All three are learned weights.

This is Bahdanau's “additive” score. Luong's simpler version is a dot product, ej = s · hj: big when the two point the same way. Transformers use a dot product too.

The score is itself a little one-hidden-layer network, trained with everything else. It's the same tanh you know from the RNN update in Part 1. A useful mental model for later: the decoder side is a "query", the encoder side is a "key", and what gets mixed are "values" (here the h_j themselves). That's exactly the vocabulary Transformers use, so it's worth naming now. In the demo, W_s and W_h each turn a 128-number memory into 64 numbers.

Step through

Translating “the black cat”, with attention

The weights here are made up to show the idea; the live demo later uses a real trained model. Step through: writing "le", it looks mostly at "the". Writing "chat", it looks at "cat", even though "cat" was read last. Writing "noir", back to "black". That's the word-order flip from Part 3 handled by looking in the right place, not by memorising the order. For <eos> the weights spread out. Compare with slide 5 of Part 3: the only new wires are the lines.

The whole decoder step

What changed from Part 3

1
Look back. Score, soften, mix, using the memory from the step before.
ct = Σj atj hj
2
Update the memory, fed the previous output and this step's context.
st = GRU( [yt−1 ; ct], st−1 )
3
Guess the next word from the memory and the context.
P(yt) = softmax( Wout [st ; ct] )
Part 3Part 4
contextone c = hT, used oncea new ct at every step
the decoder sees the inputonly through s0at every step, all of it
[a ; b] means "glue the two lists of numbers end to end". The decoder still starts from s_0 = h_T in our demo, as in Part 3, so attention adds to the old model rather than replacing it. Everything else is the same: teacher forcing, the loss, greedy and beam search. Ask: "how many weights does attention add?" In the demo, about 16,000 on top of about 180,000: W_s, W_h and v.

Why it trains better, too

A short path back for blame

Part 3: blame for a wrong day travels back through every decoder step, through c, then back through every encoder step to the 23 it came from. It fades on the way, as in Part 2.

With attention: every output step is wired straight to every hj. Blame reaches the 23 in one hop.

This links to Part 2. The LSTM's cell state was a protected path for blame through time. Attention is another kind of shortcut: no matter how long the input, each input memory is one step away from each output. This is a big part of why attention models learn long inputs faster, not just why they work better once trained. The cost: the decoder now does T scores at every step, so work grows with input length × output length.

What it learns

Alignment comes for free

Plot the weights: one row per word written, one column per word read. Bright squares are where it looked.

The diagonal is word-by-word translation. Where French puts the adjectives after the noun, the bright squares cross over.

Nobody labelled which words match. The model learned it, because looking in the right place lowers the loss.

This is redrawn from the famous figure in Bahdanau et al. (2014): "the European Economic Area" → "la zone économique européenne". The values here are illustrative, the shape is the paper's. A bonus: attention maps make the model easier to inspect. You can see where it looked when it made a mistake. Caveat if asked: attention weights aren't a complete explanation of a model's decision, but they're a useful window.

Demo · same task, same exam

The date translator, with attention

Same data as Part 3: random dates from 1900–2079 in six formats, with every 10th day and the years 2080–2099 held back.

Same GRU encoder and GRU decoder, 128 numbers per memory. The only addition: the decoder looks back at all hj, adding 16,512 weights (200,590 in all).

uv run demo/attention.py train
uv run demo/attention.py test
uv run demo/attention.py translate \
  "23 Oct 2026" --details
examPart 3 · one cPart 4 · attention
dates it never saw · 1900–2079100%100%
years it never saw · 2080–2099, in digits10.5%99.9%
years it never saw · spelled out20.3%99.3%

Part 3 had never written 208x or 209x, so it wrote a year it knew. With attention, the decoder can look at the 9 in “2091” and copy it.

Numbers from one run each (seed 0) of demo/seq2seq.py test and demo/attention.py test: 39,444 inputs from unseen days, 43,836 from unseen years. The headline is the unseen years: 12% overall for Part 3, 99.8% with attention. We didn't design attention to fix that; it's a side effect. Without attention, the decoder had to rebuild "2091" from a 128-number summary, and it had never had to rebuild a 209x before. With attention, writing the third digit, it can point at the input position holding the 9 and pass on what is there. Ask: "is that a rule now?" Not quite: the remaining mistakes are things like 2094 written as 2994. Same training recipe; the extra 16,512 weights are W_s, W_h and v. Training reaches 100% on the validation dates after about 500 rounds.

Demo · live

Watch where it looks

What to write next?

This runs the real trained model in the browser. Each row is one character written; each column is one character read; the darker the square, the more weight. Play "23 Oct 2026": it writes the year first, looking at 2, 0, 2, 6 one by one, then jumps back to "Oct" for the month, then to "23" for the day. That's the order flip, done by looking. Interesting detail: for the month it looks at the "c" of "Oct", and in "March" at the "r": the encoder reads left to right, so the memory after "Mar" is the first one that rules out "May". Same for the spelled-out year: the "w" of "two" separates it from "three". Then 2091: it has never written that year, but it copies the 9 and the 1. Finally the trap, 23/10/2026: day and year are copied right, but no training format writes the month as a number, so it writes 12. Attention lets it copy; it doesn't teach it what a month number means. Click any row label to see that step's top guesses.

Demo · the bottleneck, again

Four dates, no single c

with attention Part 3 · one c

This is the --max-dates 4 model, live: it was trained on inputs of 1 to 4 dates. Each row is one character written (tiny, there are 44 of them), each column one character read. Look at the shape: four blocks, one per date, marching left to right down the map, and inside each block the same "year, then month, then day" jump backwards you saw on the last slide. The decoder finds date 3 by looking at date 3. The line underneath is what Part 3's model wrote for this same input: the first date right, then garbage, because dates 2 to 4 had to come out of the same 128 numbers. Edit the input: delete a date, add one, change a year to 2097. Up to 4 dates; it was never trained on 5.

Demo · measured

More dates, no bottleneck

Same models, same exam as Part 3: 3,000 inputs per row, all built from dates neither model saw. Whole answer right:

dates per inputPart 3 · one c of 128Part 4 · attention
1 date · ~19 characters99.3%100%
2 dates · ~41 characters0.6%100%
3 dates · ~62 characters0%100%
4 dates · ~83 characters0%100%

Same encoder, same decoder, same 128 numbers per memory. The difference is that the decoder no longer needs one c to hold everything.

From demo/seq2seq.py and demo/attention.py, each run as train --max-dates 4 then test --max-dates 4 (seed 0). Part 3's model gets the first date right and garbles the rest; a 4× bigger c only got two dates to 20%. Attention gets every date right in every position: 100% on all 12,000 test inputs. Honest caveats if asked: this is a tidy task where each output character has one obvious place to look, which suits attention perfectly; real translation is messier. And the cost is real: training the 4-date attention model takes about 14 minutes on a laptop, against about 5 for Part 3's, because every decoder step now scores every input character. Short of time? --steps 1000 trains in about a quarter of the time and still gets 98–99.5% on every row.

The catch

What attention doesn't fix

  1. More work for long inputs. Every output step scores every input position: T × T′ scores per sentence (T characters in, T′ out). Part 3 did no extra work at all.
  2. The encoder is still an RNN. It reads one character at a time, and step t can't start until step t − 1 is done. Training can't use a GPU's thousands of cores in parallel along the sentence.
  3. It still learns patterns, not rules. Given 23/10/2026, a format it never saw, it copies the day and the year but writes the month as 12. It can copy; it doesn't know what a month number means.
Point 1 is usually fine for sentences; it becomes a problem for very long documents, and the same is true for Transformers. Point 2 is the one that changed history: if attention already connects every output to every input directly, do we still need the RNN that reads in order? Point 3 is the honest limit from the live demo: attention made copying easy, which fixed the unseen years, but nothing in the training data says that "10" in that position is October.

Where this went

2017: keep the attention, drop the recurrence

RNN encoder–decoder + attentionTransformer
reads the inputone position at a time, in orderall positions at once
remembers orderby the order it reads ina position number added to each input
attentiondecoder → encoder onlyalso every input position → every other (self-attention)
path between two far-apart wordsmany steps through the RNNone step
training on a GPUsequential along the sentenceparallel

Attention started as a fix for one c. It turned out to be the useful part.

This is as deep as the course goes into Transformers: the "why attention replaced recurrence" comparison from the mission. Self-attention is the same score–soften–mix, but every position of a sentence looks at every other position of the same sentence, so the encoder no longer needs a hidden state passed along. Order has to be put back in explicitly, as position information. Recurrence isn't dead: RNN-like models are still used where you must process a stream one step at a time with fixed memory, such as on-device speech, and newer "state space" models revive the idea. But almost every large language model today is a Transformer.

Be ready to answer

Questions

  1. What problem does attention solve? (one fixed-size c for any length; the decoder couldn't look back at the input)
  2. What are the three steps at each decoder step? (score every encoder memory, softmax into weights, weighted sum into ct)
  3. Who decides where the model looks? (nobody: the weights are learned from the translation loss alone)
  4. Why does attention also help training? (every input memory is one hop from every output step, so blame doesn't fade)
  5. What does an attention map show? (for each output word, how much weight each input word got)
  6. Why did Transformers drop the RNN? (attention already links every word directly; without recurrence, training runs in parallel)
Cover the hints, ask each question cold, and have someone answer out loud in one or two sentences. Question 2 should come with the equation: c_t = Σ a_tj h_j.

Recap

Remember:

  1. Keep every encoder memory hj, not just the last.
  2. At each decoder step: score each hj, soften the scores with softmax, mix them into a fresh ct.
  3. The weights are learned, show where the model looked, and give blame a short path back. The Transformer keeps them and drops the RNN.
Ask someone to draw slide 8 from memory: the encoder row, the decoder row, and the attention lines for one step, with the c_t equation.

End of the course

From one memory to looking back at all of them

Part 1: a hidden state. Part 2: gates to protect it. Part 3: two RNNs and a context. Part 4: attention.

Questions?

One sentence per part, as a closing recap of the whole course. If there's time, ask: "which of the four ideas survives in a Transformer?" Attention directly; gating in a different form (residual connections play a similar role to the LSTM's belt); the encoder–decoder shape in the original Transformer.
